title: Review: DNA replication; Food tests and chromatography; How enzymes work
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM09a#t2 term and clue written for the game; EZ01a#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE01b#t3 term and clue written for the game; EZ01a#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM09a#N.14, BM09b#N.4, EZ01a#N.10a, GE01b#N.7, BM09a#N.4b, EZ01a#N.11, GE01b#N.9, EZ01a#N.2a, GE01b#N.10. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Benedict's reagent
items.clue: Blue Cu²⁺ solution; forms a brick-red precipitate when heated with lactose

items.label: Metabolism
items.clue: All the chemical reactions in an organism, forming a network of linked pathways.

items.label: Density gradient
items.clue: Spun salt solution in which DNA settles at its own level, heavier DNA lower down.

items.label: Specificity
items.clue: Property by which each enzyme acts on one reaction, or on a few very similar ones.

questions.stem: A sample of milk is tested. Heated with Benedict's reagent: an orange-red precipitate. With biuret reagent: lilac. With iodine in potassium iodide: stays orange-brown. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: It contains glucose and no other sugar.
It contains starch, protein and a reducing sugar.
It contains a reducing sugar and protein, but no detectable lipid.
It contains a reducing sugar and protein, but no detectable starch.

questions.explanation: Precipitate: reducing sugar. Lilac: peptide bonds, so protein. No blue-black: no starch detected.

questions.stem: On a paper chromatogram of leaf pigments, the origin line was 20 mm from the bottom edge of the paper, the centre of the carotene spot was 65 mm from the bottom edge and the solvent front was 70 mm from the bottom edge. What is the Rf value of carotene?
questions.explanation: From the origin, the pigment moved 65 − 20 = 45 mm and the solvent front 70 − 20 = 50 mm. Rf = 45 ÷ 50 = 0.90.

questions.stem: Lipase catalyses the hydrolysis of triglycerides but has no effect on starch. What is the reason?

options.text: Starch molecules are too large to enter the active site, but any molecule smaller than starch could.
The active site of lipase is complementary in shape and chemical properties to a triglyceride only.
Starch requires more energy to break down than lipase is able to supply to the reaction.
Lipase seeks out triglyceride molecules in the fluid and ignores starch molecules it meets.

questions.explanation: Specificity arises from the structure of the active site: its shape and chemical properties match one substrate, so starch cannot bind in a way that allows catalysis.

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA molecule in which both strands contain only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) is replicated three times in a medium that supplies only light nitrogen (¹⁴N), producing 8 DNA molecules. How many of the 8 DNA molecules contain any ¹⁵N?

options.text: 1 of 8
8 of 8
2 of 8
4 of 8

questions.explanation: In round 1 the two ¹⁵N strands separate and each pairs with a new ¹⁴N strand. They stay intact in every later round, so after round 3, 2 molecules contain ¹⁵N and 6 contain only ¹⁴N.

questions.stem: Four solutions, W, X, Y and Z, were each heated with the same volume of Benedict's reagent for the same time. Final colours: W orange, X blue, Y brick red, Z green. Which list puts them in order of reducing sugar concentration, lowest first?

options.text: Y, W, Z, X
X, Z, W, Y
X, W, Z, Y
Z, X, W, Y

questions.explanation: Blue (none) → green → orange → brick red (most). The more reducing sugar, the more Cu²⁺ is reduced to red copper(I) oxide.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical bacterium, enzyme E catalyses the conversion of compound A to compound B. The conversion of A to B releases energy. A mutation stops the bacterium from making enzyme E. No other enzyme in the bacterium acts on compound A. Which prediction about compound B in the mutant bacterium is best supported?

options.text: B no longer forms at all, as A cannot change into B without enzyme E.
B forms at the normal rate, as the bacterium makes a new enzyme because it needs B.
B forms at the normal rate, as ATP supplies the energy that enzyme E used to supply.
B still forms, but far more slowly, as the reaction is no longer catalysed.

questions.stem: In the Meselson–Stahl experiment, which result after one generation in ¹⁴N would have supported the conservative model?

options.text: One band, of intermediate density.
Two bands of equal amount, one heavy and one light.
One band, heavy.
Two bands of equal amount, one intermediate and one light.

questions.explanation: Conservative keeps the parent molecule whole (heavy) and makes a completely new one (light): two bands, equal amounts.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?

options.text: It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.
It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.

questions.explanation: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.

questions.stem: The experiment is run in reverse. Bacteria are grown for many generations on light nitrogen (¹⁴N), then moved to a medium containing only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N). Replication is semi-conservative. What will the DNA show after two generations on ¹⁵N?

options.text: Two bands of equal amount: intermediate and light.
Two bands of equal amount: intermediate and heavy.
One band, between intermediate and heavy.
Two bands: one quarter light, three quarters heavy.

questions.explanation: Generation 1: every molecule is one light + one heavy strand (intermediate). Generation 2: 4 molecules, 2 hybrids holding the old light strands and 2 all-heavy.
